name: Pacifism
summary: Pacifism opposes war and, in its stronger forms, all killing and violence, holding that disputes and injustices should be met by nonviolent means such as persuasion, noncooperation and civil disobedience. It ranges from absolute pacifism, which rules out violence even in self-defence, to contingent or pragmatic forms that reject war but allow some personal defence. Its roots are religious (Christian non-resistance, ahimsa) and it has liberal, anarchist and institutional variants.

sources.usedFor: Radical pacifism's own statement: non-resistance, security, disarmament, alliances and an international police.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Peace Pledge Union's Encyclopaedia lists disarmament, unilateral if necessary, among pacifism's political implications (article 'Political Implications of Pacifism') and says the bomber fleet should be scrapped (article 'Defence'); Holmes's New Wars for Old (ch. 'A Statement of the Problem', pp. 31-33) wants states' arms transferred completely away from them.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines pacifism as the view that arbitration should be used to resolve disputes, and Britannica says pacifist organisations called for special courts to hear international conflicts.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Britannica defines pacifism as principled opposition to war and violence as a means of settling disputes, and arming insurgents to fight a government is a means of waging war.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: The Stanford entry says absolute pacifists reject even military action against dictators, while contingent pacifists accept some defensive force and others propose a nonviolent army for national defence.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: The Stanford entry says pacifists hold that killing noncombatants in war is always wrong, going beyond even the just war tradition's noncombatant immunity.

collective-defense.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says collective security means opposed alliances and its military sanctions are plain war, and the War Resisters' declaration refuses support for any war, defensive included (articles 'Sanctions', 'International Police Force'; Statement of Principles).

conscription.rationale: The Stanford entry says conscription runs counter to respect for persons, a deontological pacifist argument, and Tolstoy's refusal of military service rejects compulsory service.

decide-locally.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says democratic principles need authority decentralized as far as possible and that executive power must be decentralized, with local and professional self-government (articles 'Political Implications of Pacifism', 'Class War').

democratic-peace.rationale: Britannica says much pacifist thought of the 17th and 18th centuries held that transferring political power from rulers to the people was a crucial step to world peace, since republics would be peaceful.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says the exclusive closed empire bloc injures the nations without empires and feeds war, and urges equal trading rights for all nations in imperial territories (articles 'Imperialism and Colonies', 'Economic Warfare').

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Britannica says pacifist advocates often assume war cannot be abandoned until the world community is organised so that it can enforce justice among its members.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Holmes says peace will not be found through alliances offensive and defensive or balances of power, and the Encyclopaedia says collective security is a system of opposed alliances (New Wars for Old, ch. 'A Statement of the Problem', p. 32; article 'Sanctions').

equal-conscription.rationale: The Encyclopaedia treats conscription of men, and the coming conscription of women, as state-imposed slavery that pacifists must resist (articles 'Liberty', 'Women in Modern War, Position of').

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Britannica defines pacifism as principled opposition to war and violence as a means of settling disputes; using military force to keep a region in a country is such use.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: The Encyclopaedia calls the tariff war a potent cause of international friction leading to armed conflict, urges lowering tariff barriers, and lists removal of barriers to international trade among pacifism's political implications (articles 'Economic Warfare', 'Political Implications of Pacifism').

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The Stanford entry says most pacifists reject nuclear war, that for Cortright pacifism is absolute on nuclear war, and that just war pacifism targets nuclear deterrence strategy.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Every form of pacifism in the Stanford entry rejects aggressive war and violence, so none holds that initiating force outside defence can be justified.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Britannica defines pacifism as principled opposition to war and violence as a means of settling disputes, and the Stanford entry says pacifists reject wars to impose a political order.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The Stanford entry says pacifists treat the peace of nuclear deterrence as no real peace, and that just war pacifism rejects nuclear deterrence strategy.

leader-cult.rationale: The Encyclopaedia lists the idolatry of the nation or a semi-deified tyrant as part of militarism and says rulers use propaganda to pass themselves off as the nation's divine person (articles 'Revolution', 'Prestige and National Honour').

limit-guns.rationale: Holmes presents loaded revolvers kept in bureau drawers as evidence of insecurity and looks to a disarmed citizenry (New Wars for Old, ch. 'A Statement of the Problem', pp. 30-33).

means-match-ends.rationale: The Stanford entry says the Gandhi-King approach stresses coordination between means and ends: peaceful means must be used in pursuit of peace and justice.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: The Stanford entry says contingent pacifists accept at most defence of self and the innocent, and pacifists reject wars fought for a just social order.

military-force-for-human-rights.rationale: The Stanford entry says pacifists hold that only nonviolent means fit the end of human rights and maximal pacifists reject military action even against human-rights violations, while noting that some pacifists accept intervention.

military-organisation-revolutionary-part.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says a revolution that is to slaughter efficiently must be organised on a military basis and so becomes a fascist dictatorship, and calls a bloody revolution a contradiction in terms (article 'Revolution').

military-superiority.rationale: The Stanford entry says pacifists reject the peace of deterrence as the product of an increase in armaments and counts arms races and the money spent preparing for war among the harms of the war system.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: The Encyclopaedia points to municipal transport, light, water and road services as examples of limiting capitalism that already work, alongside the co-operative movement (article 'Economic Implications of Pacifism').

nation-first.rationale: The Encyclopaedia calls nationalism a form of idolatry, holds that Britain should disarm and open its trade unilaterally, and sets pacifism against nationalism (articles 'Nationalistic Religion', 'Economic Warfare', 'Political Implications of Pacifism').

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The Stanford entry says some absolute pacifists reject even personal self-defence, while others and contingent pacifists such as Cortright accept force for self-defence.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: The Stanford entry says most pacifists reject nuclear war and Britannica ties pacifism to the movement to abolish nuclear weapons, which rules out basing them anywhere.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says pacifism is incompatible with any tyranny, that its political philosophy is democratic, and that pacifists should refuse to join parties pledged to intolerance (articles 'Political Implications of Pacifism', 'Economic Implications of Pacifism', 'Civil War').

party-controls-media.rationale: The Encyclopaedia condemns the official censorship of the totalitarian states as part of the preparation for war, and calls state and plutocratic control of the press thoroughly vicious (article 'Propaganda').

people-in-arms.rationale: Holmes holds that a disarmed citizenry is the road to peace and that bolts, revolvers and armed guards breed insecurity (New Wars for Old, ch. 'A Statement of the Problem', pp. 30-32), and the Encyclopaedia condemns drilling civilians for war (articles 'Liberty' and 'Women in Modern War').

person-over-state.rationale: The Stanford entry says pacifists object that war and conscription treat persons as means or interchangeable cogs, and Holmes's deontological pacifism makes individuals the focus of morality rather than collectives.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Britannica defines pacifism as principled opposition to war and violence as a means of settling disputes, and states the principle of nonviolence as that violence of any kind is always wrong.

publish-international-agreements.rationale: The Encyclopaedia cites the secret treaties of 1915-17 as showing that once war starts all considerations of justice vanish, and points readers to the Union of Democratic Control's work against them (article 'Secret Treaties').

religious-offensive-war.rationale: Britannica defines pacifism as principled opposition to war, and the Stanford entry says pacifists reject wars fought to impose a just order; a war to extend one religion's rule is such a war.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: The Stanford entry says most pacifists actively resist evil nonviolently and absolute pacifism may require self-sacrifice, while Tolstoy holds that the only deliverance from violence is its submissive endurance.

sacred-nation.rationale: The Encyclopaedia calls the deification of the country idolatry that is philosophically absurd and disastrous, and says the nation is not a person with a will of its own (articles 'Patriotism', 'Prestige and National Honour').

socialism-needs-revolutionary-war.rationale: The Encyclopaedia argues that violence cannot make a genuine revolution or defend socialism, and that only non-violent resistance will not turn a socialist community into its opposite (article 'Revolution').

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Tolstoy argues that Christians must refuse military service, and Britannica holds that participation in any act of war is wrong for individual pacifists, though the Stanford entry says particular pacifists do not condemn soldiers who fight.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Holmes accepts, as a necessary qualification for groups, a police system that takes all agencies of force from private citizens and restricts them to a picked body serving the community (New Wars for Old, ch. 'A Statement of the Problem', pp. 32-33).

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Holmes rejects alliances and balances of power as ways to peace, and the Encyclopaedia describes collective security as opposed alliances that make a war between two groups of allied powers (New Wars for Old, ch. 'A Statement of the Problem', p. 32; article 'Sanctions').

strong-leader.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says the power any one individual can wield must be strictly limited, and that pacifism is incompatible with any form of tyranny (article 'Political Implications of Pacifism').

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says tariffs strangle trade and that the alternative to economic disarmament is intensified tariff war ending in armed conflict, so it wants barriers removed, by Britain first if need be (article 'Economic Warfare').

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Encyclopaedia condemns imperialism's pride in size and force, names the pursuit of territory as a cause of war, and lists liquidation of empire among pacifism's political implications (articles 'Imperialism and Colonies', 'Causes of War', 'Political Implications of Pacifism').

total-state.rationale: The Encyclopaedia says war preparation of the kind that makes a country one vast barracks destroys liberty, and that pacifism means decentralized democratic institutions (articles 'Liberty', 'Political Implications of Pacifism').

uniformed-youth.rationale: The Encyclopaedia condemns rifle drill and military training of children in the dictatorial states as education for war and slavery (articles 'Education and Peace', 'Liberty').

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Britannica defines pacifism as principled opposition to war and violence as a means of settling disputes, and the Stanford entry argues violent revolution tends to escalate oppression.

war-builds-character.rationale: Britannica lists the moral and spiritual degradation war brings among the central arguments for pacifism, and the Stanford entry counts war's damage to culture and political life among its harms.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The Encyclopaedia calls industrial organizations miniature dictatorships and wants decentralization into self-governing groups in all trades and professions (article 'Political Implications of Pacifism').

missingStatements.rationale: Absolute and most principled pacifists hold that war is always wrong, though contingent pacifists reject only particular wars.

scope: Pacifism as the Stanford Encyclopedia (s2), Britannica (s5) and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (s6) define it: opposition to war and, in its absolute form, to all violence, ranging from absolute pacifism through contingent or conditional pacifism to pragmatic and nonviolent-resistance forms, with religious, liberal, feminist and institutional variants. Gandhian nonviolence and the Tolstoyan movement are separate ideologies with their own entries and are not taken as part of this scope.
